intro.title: How This Calculator Evaluates an Expression
intro.paragraph1: This calculator evaluates operations the way a physical scientific calculator does: sequentially, as you enter them, rather than parsing a fully typed-out expression with parentheses. Pressing an operator immediately resolves whatever calculation is pending, then queues the new one; pressing a function key (sin, √x, ln, and the rest) applies instantly to the number currently on screen. This covers four families of operations — basic arithmetic, powers and roots, logarithms and exponentials, and trigonometry — each accessible from the keypad without switching modes.
intro.paragraph2: Two details matter for getting a correct result. First, the Deg/Rad toggle changes how every trigonometric and inverse-trigonometric function interprets its input and output — the same button sequence gives a different numeric answer in each mode, so it's worth checking before reading a trig result. Second, some inputs have no real answer at all: dividing by zero, taking the square root or logarithm of a negative number, or asking for the arcsine of a value outside −1 to 1. Rather than returning an invalid number silently, this calculator flags these as explicit errors so a wrong input is never mistaken for a real result.

items.question: Why do I get a different answer for the same trig calculation sometimes?
items.answer: Almost always it's the Deg/Rad toggle — the same key sequence evaluates to a different number depending on whether the calculator is currently interpreting angles in degrees or radians. This calculator defaults to degrees; check the mode indicator in the top-left of the keypad before reading a trigonometric result.

items.question: Why does dividing by zero show an error instead of a number?
items.answer: Division by zero, the square root or logarithm of a negative number, and the arcsine or arccosine of a value outside −1 to 1 have no real numeric answer. Rather than silently returning something like Infinity or NaN, this calculator surfaces these as explicit errors so an invalid input is never mistaken for a real result.

items.question: What does the "Ans" key do?
items.answer: It recalls the result of your last completed calculation, letting you feed it straight into a new expression without retyping the number.

items.question: What's the difference between memory (M+/M−/MR) and Ans?
items.answer: Ans always holds only your very last result and updates every time you calculate something new. Memory is a separate, persistent slot you control explicitly — useful for accumulating a running subtotal across several unrelated calculations without it being overwritten by whatever you compute next.

items.question: Why doesn't this calculator support typing a full expression with parentheses?
items.answer: It follows the same immediate, sequential evaluation model as most physical scientific calculators: each operator resolves the pending calculation right away rather than waiting to parse a complete expression. This matches the keypad layout and behavior calculator users already know, at the cost of not supporting parenthesized grouping.

history.title: From the Slide Rule to the Shirt Pocket
history.paragraph: For centuries, the slide rule was the only practical portable tool for trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential calculations — the pocket calculators that existed by the late 1960s could only add, subtract, multiply, and divide. That changed in 1972, when Hewlett-Packard released the HP-35, conceived after company co-founder Bill Hewlett asked whether the scientific functions of HP's desktop calculators could be squeezed into something that fit in a shirt pocket. It was the first handheld calculator to compute trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions directly, and it caught on immediately: HP sold more than 300,000 units in its first three years, and the HP-35's descendants went on to sell over 20 million units — making the slide rule obsolete for the engineers and scientists who had relied on it for generations.

modernDevelopments.title: From Dedicated Hardware to the Browser
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Scientific calculators kept evolving after the HP-35 — graphing and computer-algebra models from makers like Texas Instruments and Casio added visual function plotting and symbolic manipulation, and calculator apps became a default feature of every computer and phone operating system. The more recent shift is calculators that need no dedicated hardware or installed app at all: modern browsers can run the same trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential computations entirely in JavaScript on the page itself, the way this tool does — every calculation happens on your own device, with nothing sent to a server.

intro.title: How an Age Calculator Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: An age calculator turns two calendar dates — a birth date and a reference date — into a precise breakdown of elapsed time. That sounds trivial until you remember that a "year" is not a fixed number of days: months run 28 to 31 days long, and February gains an extra day every leap year. Getting years, months, and days exactly right means walking the calendar day by day in software, not just subtracting two numbers.
intro.paragraph2: This tool computes that breakdown down to the second, then layers on context most simple age calculators skip entirely: a Hijri (Islamic) calendar age, a generation label, zodiac signs, and a live countdown to your next birthday.
intro.disclaimer: This tool calculates chronological (calendar) age only. It is not a substitute for biological, developmental, or medical age assessments, which a qualified professional determines using different methods entirely.

calculationMethod.title: How to Calculate Age From a Date of Birth, Step by Step
calculationMethod.intro: The years-months-days breakdown is computed with calendar subtraction: start from the reference date and count backward, borrowing from the next-larger unit whenever a smaller one would go negative — the same logic you'd use counting on your fingers, just automated.
calculationMethod.borrowingExplanation: If the reference date's day-of-month is earlier than the birth date's day-of-month, you borrow a month (adding however many days that borrowed month actually has); if the reference date's month is earlier than the birth month, you borrow a year. This is why the calculation can't be a simple average — the number of days in the borrowed month changes the result.

culturalReckoning.title: Not Every Culture Counts Age the Same Way
culturalReckoning.intro: The "years since birth, incrementing on your birthday" method used above — sometimes called international age — is the global default today, but it is a relatively recent standard even in places that now use it exclusively.

hijri.title: The Hijri (Islamic) Calendar
hijri.paragraph: The Hijri calendar is purely lunar, with 12 months of 29 or 30 days totaling about 354–355 days a year — roughly 11 days shorter than the Gregorian solar year. Because of that gap, a person's age in Hijri years is consistently a few percent higher than their age in Gregorian years, and Hijri dates drift earlier through the Gregorian seasons over a person's lifetime. This calculator's Hijri age uses the tabular (civil) Islamic calendar, a fixed mathematical approximation used by most software calendars — it can differ by a day or two from the real, moon-sighting-based calendar used for religious observances.

korea.title: South Korea's Recent Switch to International Age
korea.paragraph: Until June 28, 2023, South Korea officially used a traditional counting-age system: a newborn was considered 1 year old at birth, and everyone gained a year on New Year's Day rather than on their individual birthday — so someone born on December 31 turned 2 the very next day under that system. A law passed by South Korea's National Assembly in December 2022 standardized the country on the international age system used in this calculator, effective from mid-2023, ending decades of most Koreans routinely being one or two "years" older by local counting than by international counting.

generationTable.title: Which Generation Were You Born In?
generationTable.intro: Generational labels are a social-research convention, not a law of nature — the ranges below follow the widely cited Pew Research Center definitions through Generation Z; the labels after that (Alpha, Beta) come from other researchers, since Pew has not published an official cutoff for them.

lifeStages.title: Life Stages and Life Expectancy
lifeStages.paragraph1: The "Life Expectancy" indicator above splits a lifespan into five consecutive, non-overlapping stages: childhood (0-9 years), adolescence (10-19, the World Health Organization's official definition), youth (20-39) and middle age (40-59) — following Erik Erikson's stages of psychosocial development — and old age (60+, WHO's definition of an "older person" for developing-country statistics).
lifeStages.paragraph2: The indicator updates with every calculation to reflect your actual age and your position on the life-expectancy scale for the selected sex, along with the approximate percentage of that average elapsed and the estimated time remaining in years, weeks and days. This is a general statistical estimate based on global population averages, not a medical prediction or diagnosis for any individual.

milestonesContext.title: Why Legal Age Milestones Vary So Much by Country
milestonesContext.paragraph: Ages like 18, 21, or 65 feel like universal constants, but almost none of them are. The age of majority is 18 in most of the world but 19 in a handful of countries and as low as 15 or as high as 21 in others; the minimum drinking age is 18 in most countries yet 21 in the United States; state pension ages range from the late 50s to the late 60s and are actively being raised in many countries as life expectancy increases. The milestone ages this tool highlights reflect common international patterns, not a single universal legal standard — always confirm the applicable age in your own jurisdiction before relying on it for a legal or administrative decision.

limitations.title: Limitations and Edge Cases
limitations.paragraph1: Anyone born on February 29 has a real, once-every-four-years birthday. In the three out of four years that aren't leap years, this calculator (like virtually all calendar software) treats their next birthday as March 1, since no February 29 exists on the calendar in that year.
limitations.paragraph2: Total hours, minutes, and seconds lived are calculated using your device's local clock and time zone at the moment you calculate — they are not adjusted for time-zone changes, travel, or daylight saving transitions across your lifetime, which would shift the true elapsed time by at most a few hours in nearly all real cases.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Age Calculation

items.question: Why does my Hijri age look higher than my Gregorian age?
items.answer: Because a Hijri year (about 354–355 days) is shorter than a Gregorian year (about 365.25 days), more Hijri years fit into the same span of real time — roughly 3% more per year of life. This is a real calendar effect, not a calculation error.

items.question: Is the Hijri date this tool shows exactly what my local mosque or country uses?
items.answer: Not necessarily. This tool uses the tabular (civil) Islamic calendar — a fixed mathematical scheme — while many countries and religious authorities set the start of each Hijri month by an actual moon sighting or a specific local authority's announcement (such as the Umm al-Qura calendar in Saudi Arabia). These can differ from the tabular calcular by a day or two.

items.question: How is my zodiac sign determined?
items.answer: From your birth month and day alone, using the standard tropical zodiac date ranges (for example, Aries runs March 21 to April 19). This is a cultural convention, not an astronomical or scientific measurement.

items.question: Can this tool calculate my age on a future date, not just today?
items.answer: Yes — enable "Calculate age as of a specific date" and enter any date on or after your date of birth, past or future. This is useful for figuring out your exact age for a visa application, an exam eligibility cutoff, or any date-specific requirement.

items.question: Why did the seconds-lived number jump by more than one when I wasn't looking?
items.answer: The live counter recalculates from your exact birth timestamp once per second; if the browser tab was in the background or your device was asleep, it simply catches up to the correct value the moment it updates again — no time is actually lost or miscounted.

items.question: Does this tool store or send my birth date anywhere?

behindTheTool.title: Behind the Tool: The Calendars and Standards Age Calculation Depends On

history.title: Why We Use the Calendar We Do: the Gregorian Reform of 1582
history.paragraph: Every calendar-based age calculation on this page ultimately rests on the Gregorian calendar, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII through the papal bull Inter gravissimas on February 24, 1582. The problem it solved was real drift: the Julian calendar's year was about 11 minutes longer than the true solar year, and over the roughly 1,257 years since the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE, that error had pushed the calendar 10 days out of sync with the seasons. The fix took effect that October: Thursday, October 4, 1582 (Julian) was followed directly by Friday, October 15, 1582 (Gregorian) — ten calendar days were simply skipped — alongside a new, more accurate leap-year rule (century years are leap years only if divisible by 400) that keeps the modern calendar aligned with the seasons to within about 26 seconds a year.

equipment.title: The Standard Behind Every Date Field: ISO 8601
equipment.paragraph: The date fields in this calculator, and in virtually every computer system that stores or exchanges dates, follow ISO 8601-1:2019, the International Organization for Standardization's formal standard for representing dates and times unambiguously (for example, 2026-08-03 instead of a locale-dependent format that could mean either August 3 or March 8). Precision at the finer end — the "live seconds" this tool ticks up every second — depends on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), maintained with reference to a global network of atomic clocks.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Timekeeping: NTP, UTC, and the End of Leap Seconds
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Your device's clock stays accurate to within a fraction of a second largely thanks to the Network Time Protocol (NTP), which continuously synchronizes it against reference time servers. Those servers ultimately trace back to UTC, whose leap-second adjustments (needed because Earth's rotation is slightly irregular) are decided by the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS). In November 2022, the 27th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) adopted Resolution 4, agreeing to increase the currently permitted UT1-UTC deviation at or before 2035 — effectively phasing out leap seconds while keeping UTC continuous for at least a century, so that timekeeping software (including tools like this one) never has to handle an actual 61-second minute.

intro.title: What Is Body Mass Index?
intro.paragraph1: Body Mass Index (BMI) is a simple screening measure that relates your weight to your height. It divides your weight in kilograms by the square of your height in meters, producing a single number that places you within a broad weight category.
intro.paragraph2: Because BMI only needs height and weight, it's widely used by clinicians and researchers as a quick, low-cost way to flag potential weight-related health risks across large populations.
intro.disclaimer: BMI is a general screening indicator, not a medical diagnosis. It doesn't account for muscle mass, bone density, or body composition — always discuss your results with a qualified healthcare professional.

Irregular menstrual cycles or fertility issues

limitations.title: Limitations of BMI
limitations.paragraph1: BMI is calculated from height and weight alone, so it cannot distinguish between weight from muscle and weight from fat. A muscular athlete and a person carrying excess body fat can share the same BMI while having very different health profiles.
limitations.paragraph2: Its interpretation also shifts with age, sex, and fitness level: older adults naturally lose muscle and gain fat at the same weight, and body-fat distribution differs between men and women. For these reasons, BMI is best used as a starting point alongside other measures — such as waist circumference, body-fat percentage, and a clinical assessment — rather than as a stand-alone verdict.

items.question: Is BMI accurate for athletes and very muscular people?
items.answer: Not always. Since BMI can't distinguish muscle from fat, athletes and people with high muscle mass often score as “overweight” or “obese” despite having low body-fat levels. Waist circumference or a body-fat measurement gives a more accurate picture in these cases.

items.question: Does BMI measure body fat directly?
items.answer: No. BMI is an indirect estimate based only on height and weight. Two people with the same BMI can have very different amounts of body fat depending on muscle mass, age, and body composition.

items.question: Is the calculation different for children and teenagers?
items.answer: Yes. Children and teens are assessed using age- and sex-specific BMI-for-age percentile charts rather than the fixed adult categories, since body composition changes significantly during growth.

items.question: Does BMI account for age or sex?
items.answer: The adult formula and category thresholds are the same for all adults aged 20 and over, regardless of sex. This is one of its main limitations, since body composition naturally differs by age and sex.

items.question: What's the difference between BMI and body fat percentage?
items.answer: BMI estimates a weight category from height and weight alone, while body-fat percentage measures the actual proportion of fat tissue in the body — usually through methods like skinfold calipers, bioelectrical impedance, or DEXA scans. Body-fat percentage is more precise but requires specialized tools.

items.question: Does a “normal” BMI automatically mean I'm healthy?
items.answer: Not necessarily. BMI is only one indicator. Factors such as diet quality, physical activity, waist circumference, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels all play an important role in overall health.

primeIndex.title: BMI Prime and the Ponderal Index
primeIndex.intro: Two related measures refine what a plain BMI number tells you: BMI Prime expresses BMI as a ratio to the upper limit of normal weight, while the Ponderal Index adjusts for height using volume instead of area — making it more reliable for very tall or short individuals.

prime.label: BMI Prime
prime.note: A BMI Prime below 1.0 falls within the normal-weight upper limit; above 1.0 indicates overweight or obesity in direct proportion to the excess.

ponderal.label: Ponderal Index
ponderal.note: Because it divides by height cubed instead of squared, the Ponderal Index scales more accurately with body volume and is often preferred in pediatric and neonatal growth assessments.

behindTheTool.title: Behind the Tool: The Story and Science of BMI

history.title: Where BMI Came From
history.paragraph: BMI traces back to the Belgian mathematician and statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who developed the weight-to-height-squared ratio in the 1830s while studying the statistical properties of the ‘average man’ across large populations. His goal wasn't individual diagnosis — it was a population-level tool to describe how body weight related to height across a society. The formula stayed largely a statistical curiosity for over a century until physiologist Ancel Keys popularized it as ‘Body Mass Index’ in a 1972 study comparing methods for estimating body fat across large groups, after finding it correlated better with body fat than competing indices of the time.

equipment.title: The Equipment Behind an Accurate Measurement
equipment.intro: A reliable BMI calculation depends on two simple but precise instruments: a calibrated medical scale and a stadiometer.

items.name: Calibrated Medical Scale
items.description: Clinical-grade scales are calibrated regularly and read in fine increments, while typical home bathroom scales can drift several hundred grams to a kilogram out of calibration over time — enough to shift a borderline BMI result into a different category.

items.name: Stadiometer (Height Gauge)
items.description: A vertical ruler with a sliding headpiece — height is more accurately measured standing barefoot against a wall-mounted stadiometer than estimated or self-reported.

modernDevelopments.title: Beyond BMI: Modern Alternatives
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Because BMI can't separate fat from muscle, clinical and research settings increasingly turn to more direct methods: DEXA (Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry) scans estimate body-fat percentage and bone density with high precision, bioelectrical impedance scales estimate body composition through a small electrical current, and waist-to-hip ratio adds a measure of fat distribution that BMI ignores entirely. These methods are more accurate but require specialized equipment, which is why BMI remains the standard first-pass screening tool.

intro.title: What This Calculator Measures
intro.paragraph1: A mortgage is a loan secured by the property you're buying, structured so that a fixed monthly payment gradually eliminates a large balance over a period typically running 15 to 30 years. Almost every fixed-rate mortgage today is fully amortizing: each payment splits between interest owed on the remaining balance and principal that permanently reduces it, and that split shifts every month — early payments are mostly interest, and the very last payment is nearly all principal.
intro.paragraph2: This calculator computes your standard monthly principal-and-interest payment from your loan amount, rate, and term, then folds in the real recurring costs lenders typically collect alongside it — property tax, home insurance, HOA dues, and private mortgage insurance (PMI) — to show the payment you'll actually see leave your account. It also runs a full month-by-month amortization simulation behind the scenes, which is what lets it tell you exactly when PMI can come off and how much an extra payment would actually save, rather than relying on rough rules of thumb.
intro.disclaimer: This tool is for planning and educational purposes only. It does not constitute a loan offer, pre-approval, or financial advice, and actual loan terms, taxes, insurance premiums, and PMI rates set by a specific lender or insurer may differ from the estimates shown here.

amortization.title: How Mortgage Amortization Works
amortization.intro: Every fixed-rate, fully amortizing loan uses the same payment formula, regardless of the lender. Given the loan principal, the periodic interest rate, and the number of payments, the formula solves for the one constant payment that brings the balance to exactly zero on the final payment.

formula.label: Standard Monthly Payment Formula
formula.note: M is the monthly principal-and-interest payment, P is the loan principal, r is the monthly interest rate (the annual rate divided by 12), and n is the total number of monthly payments (the loan term in years times 12). When r = 0, the formula reduces to simple division: M = P / n.

example.title: Worked Example
example.intro: Take this calculator's own defaults: a $400,000 home with a 20% down payment, a 6.5% annual rate, and a 30-year term.
example.result: Over 360 payments, that totals $728,142.36 paid — $320,000 of principal and $408,142.36 of interest, roughly 1.28× the loan amount, before taxes, insurance, HOA, or PMI are even added.

paymentComponents.title: What Makes Up Your Monthly Payment
paymentComponents.intro: The number a lender actually asks you to pay each month — sometimes called PITI — is rarely just principal and interest. This calculator breaks it into every component that commonly makes up a US mortgage payment:

items.label: Principal & Interest (P&I)
items.description: The fixed payment computed by the amortization formula above — the only component that actually retires the loan.

items.label: Property Tax
items.description: Billed annually by the local government based on the assessed value of the home; most lenders collect a twelfth of the annual bill each month and pay the tax authority directly from an escrow account.

items.label: Home Insurance
items.description: Hazard insurance protecting the physical structure, required by virtually every lender as a condition of the loan and typically collected monthly through the same escrow account as property tax.

items.label: HOA Fees
items.description: A due paid directly to a homeowners' association when the property belongs to one — not collected by the lender, but included here because it's a real recurring cost of owning the home.

items.label: Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI)
items.description: Required on most conventional loans when the down payment is below 20%; it protects the lender, not the borrower, against default — see below for exactly when it can be removed.

pmi.title: Private Mortgage Insurance: What It Is and How to Remove It
pmi.intro: PMI isn't an optional add-on the borrower chooses — on a conventional loan, a lender is required to charge it whenever the down payment is below 20% (equivalently, the loan-to-value ratio is above 80%), because it protects the lender's exposure if the borrower defaults early, when equity is thin. Two exact thresholds are set by name in US federal law, the Homeowners Protection Act of 1998 (12 U.S.C. § 4902):

rows.label: Borrower-Requested Cancellation
rows.note: Once your scheduled balance is projected to reach 80% of the home's original value, you can submit a written request to your servicer to cancel PMI, provided your payment history is current (12 U.S.C. § 4902(a)).

rows.label: Automatic Termination
rows.note: Even if you never ask, the servicer is legally required to automatically terminate PMI once your balance is first scheduled to reach 78% of the original value, as long as payments are current (12 U.S.C. § 4902(b)).

pmi.note: Both thresholds are based on the home's original value and the loan's original amortization schedule — not on extra payments or market appreciation, unless you separately request a new appraisal-based cancellation. This calculator's “PMI Removal” estimate reflects the scheduled 80% threshold, adjusted for any extra monthly payment you've entered.

extraPayments.title: The Real Impact of Paying a Little Extra Each Month
extraPayments.intro: Because interest is charged only on the remaining balance, every extra dollar applied to principal today stops accruing interest for every remaining month of the loan — which is why even a modest recurring overpayment compounds into a disproportionately large reduction in total interest and loan term.

example.result: That single, consistent $200/month habit saves $105,428.67 in interest — over 500 times the $200 itself, repeated across the shortened loan term.

rateTypes.title: Fixed-Rate vs. Adjustable-Rate Mortgages
rateTypes.intro: This calculator models a fixed-rate mortgage, the dominant structure for US home loans, but it's worth understanding the alternative you'll encounter when comparing loan offers:

fixed.title: Fixed-Rate Mortgage (FRM)
fixed.paragraph: The interest rate is locked for the entire loan term, so the principal-and-interest portion of the payment never changes — only the escrowed taxes, insurance, and PMI can shift the total bill over time. This predictability is why fixed-rate loans, especially the 30-year term, have been the default choice for most US homebuyers since the government-backed reforms of the 1930s standardized amortizing mortgages.

adjustable.title: Adjustable-Rate Mortgage (ARM)
adjustable.paragraph: The rate is fixed for an initial period (commonly 5, 7, or 10 years, as in a “7/1 ARM”), then adjusts periodically based on a reference index plus a lender margin, subject to caps that limit how much it can move at each adjustment and over the life of the loan. ARMs often start below prevailing fixed rates, trading long-term predictability for a lower initial payment.

limitations.title: Limitations of This Calculator
limitations.paragraph1: This tool assumes a fixed interest rate for the full term, a home value that doesn't change, and property tax, insurance, and HOA amounts that stay constant in nominal terms — none of which is guaranteed in practice. Property taxes are typically reassessed periodically, insurance premiums are repriced at renewal, and PMI can sometimes be removed earlier via a new appraisal showing sufficient value gain, none of which this calculator can predict.
limitations.paragraph2: It also excludes one-time costs that are very real parts of buying a home but aren't part of the recurring monthly payment: closing costs, loan origination fees, title insurance, and any upfront mortgage insurance premium some loan programs charge. Treat every figure here as a planning estimate, not a lender's official Loan Estimate or Closing Disclosure.

items.question: Why does my total interest look larger than my loan amount?
items.answer: On long terms at typical rates, this is normal, not an error: a 30-year loan at 6.5% pays roughly 1.28× the principal in interest by the time the amortization example above finishes. Interest is charged on whatever balance remains, and early in the loan almost the entire balance remains, so a large share of your early payments is interest rather than principal.

items.question: Does this calculator include closing costs?
items.answer: No. It computes only the recurring monthly payment components — principal, interest, taxes, insurance, HOA, and PMI. One-time costs like closing costs, appraisal fees, and title insurance are outside this tool's scope; see Limitations above.

items.question: Is PMI the same as homeowners insurance?
items.answer: No — they protect different parties. Homeowners insurance protects you against physical damage to the home. PMI protects only the lender against your default, and it doesn't pay out to you or repair anything if you file a claim.

items.question: Can I remove PMI before the scheduled 80% threshold?
items.answer: Often, yes. If your home's value has risen since purchase — through appreciation or improvements — you can typically request a new appraisal and ask your servicer to cancel PMI once the current, appraised loan-to-value ratio reaches 80%, without waiting for the scheduled balance to get there on its own. This calculator only models the scheduled path, since it can't predict future appraisals.

items.question: Why do extra payments save so much more interest than their dollar amount?
items.answer: Because interest compounds on the balance every month for the remaining life of the loan. A dollar of extra principal paid in year 2 stops accruing interest for the other 28 years it would otherwise have remained outstanding — see the worked example above.

items.question: What's the difference between loan-to-value (LTV) and down payment percent?
items.answer: They're complementary: LTV is the loan amount divided by the home price, and down payment percent is the down payment divided by the home price. A 20% down payment corresponds exactly to an 80% LTV — the same line lenders use to decide whether PMI applies.

behindTheTool.title: Behind the Tool: The History and Standards Behind the Modern Mortgage

history.title: From Balloon Payments to the Amortized Mortgage: The Reforms of 1933–1934
history.paragraph: Before the 1930s, the typical US home loan looked nothing like today's mortgage: it ran just 5 to 10 years, charged interest-only payments, and ended in a single “balloon” payment of the full principal — a structure that triggered a wave of foreclosures once the Great Depression made refinancing that balloon impossible for millions of homeowners. Congress responded on June 13, 1933 by creating the Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC), which refinanced roughly one million troubled mortgages between 1933 and 1936 using a new structure: a longer, self-amortizing loan in which every payment stayed level and gradually retired the entire principal, eliminating the balloon altogether. The National Housing Act of 1934 then created the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), which insured lenders against default and extended the amortizing structure to 25- and 30-year terms — the direct ancestor of the fixed-rate mortgage this calculator models.

equipment.title: The Standard Behind PMI Removal: The Homeowners Protection Act of 1998
equipment.paragraph: The exact thresholds this calculator uses to estimate when PMI can come off aren't a rule of thumb — they're set in US federal law. The Homeowners Protection Act of 1998 (12 U.S.C. § 4902), signed July 29, 1998 and effective July 29, 1999, requires a servicer to automatically terminate PMI on a conventional loan once the principal balance is first scheduled to reach 78% of the property's original value (§ 4902(b)), and separately gives borrowers in good standing the right to request cancellation once the balance is scheduled to reach 80% (§ 4902(a)) — the same two figures behind this tool's “PMI Removal” estimate.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Mortgage Technology: Automated Valuation and Digital Closings
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Two shifts have reshaped mortgage underwriting and closing in recent years. Automated valuation models (AVMs) now estimate a property's value from county records, comparable sales, and increasingly satellite imagery and computer vision, letting many lenders waive an in-person appraisal for well-documented properties under roughly $250,000–$400,000. And remote online notarization (RON) — now legally recognized in more than 40 US states — lets a borrower sign closing documents in front of a notary over live video instead of at an in-person closing table. Industry surveys report a majority of borrowers now upload documents and e-sign through digital portals rather than in person, a shift that has measurably shortened the closing timeline this calculator's numbers ultimately feed into.

intro.title: What Cryptocurrency and Blockchain Are
intro.paragraph1: A cryptocurrency is a digital asset recorded on a blockchain — a shared, append-only ledger maintained by a network of independent computers rather than a single bank or government. Ownership is tracked through cryptographic keys instead of a central account database, and new entries are added only when the network's participants agree they are valid, following rules set by the underlying protocol rather than a central authority.
intro.paragraph2: This page uses live, public market data to show current prices, a converter between any two of the top cryptocurrencies by market capitalization, historical price charts, and a calculator that shows how a hypothetical past purchase would have changed in value by today, based on real historical prices — a purely informational and educational presentation, not a trading platform or a source of investment recommendations.
intro.disclaimer: The material below explains general concepts and verifiable historical facts. It does not constitute investment, legal, or tax advice, and nothing here should be read as encouragement to buy, sell, or hold any specific asset.

blockchain.title: How a Blockchain Works
blockchain.paragraph1: A blockchain groups transactions into blocks, and each block includes a cryptographic hash — a fixed-length fingerprint computed from its own contents — of the block immediately before it. That link is what gives the structure its name and its tamper-evidence: changing anything in an earlier block would change its hash, which would no longer match the copy stored in the next block, breaking the chain in a way every participant in the network can detect.
blockchain.paragraph2: New blocks are added only when the network reaches agreement through a consensus mechanism. Bitcoin uses Proof of Work, where computers compete to solve a computationally expensive puzzle before adding the next block; Ethereum and most newer networks use Proof of Stake, where participants lock up ("stake") some of the network's own currency as a financial commitment backing the blocks they propose.

risks.title: The Real Risks of Holding Cryptocurrency
risks.paragraph1: Price volatility in cryptocurrency markets is substantially higher than in most traditional asset classes — double-digit percentage price swings within a single day are not unusual, driven by relatively thin liquidity, sentiment shifts, and the absence of the circuit breakers many traditional exchanges use.
risks.paragraph2: Regulatory treatment varies widely by country and continues to change: some jurisdictions have established clear licensing and tax frameworks, others restrict or ban certain activities outright, and many are still actively developing their approach — a legal status that can shift with little notice.
risks.paragraph3: Custody carries its own distinct risk: cryptographic keys held directly by an individual cannot be recovered if lost, and funds held on an exchange or other third-party platform depend on that platform's own security and solvency.

items.question: Is a cryptocurrency the same thing as a blockchain?
items.answer: No. A blockchain is the underlying ledger technology; a cryptocurrency is one application of it — the digital asset whose ownership and transfer that ledger records. Blockchains are also used for purposes unrelated to currency, such as recording supply-chain data or digital certificates.

items.question: Why do cryptocurrency prices change so much within a single day?
items.answer: Cryptocurrency markets trade continuously, every day of the year, with no single central exchange and comparatively thin liquidity for all but the largest coins by market capitalization — conditions that let relatively small trades move the price more than they would in larger, more liquid traditional markets.

items.question: What does "market capitalization" mean for a cryptocurrency?
items.answer: It's the current price multiplied by the circulating supply — the total number of coins that exist and are publicly available, excluding any that are locked, reserved, or not yet issued.

history.title: Origins: Satoshi Nakamoto and the Bitcoin Whitepaper
history.paragraph: On October 31, 2008, a person or group using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto published a nine-page paper titled "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System" to a cryptography mailing list, describing a way for two parties to transact directly online without relying on a trusted financial intermediary. The Bitcoin network itself went live on January 3, 2009, with the mining of its first block, known as the genesis block. Nakamoto's real identity has never been confirmed, and remained active in the project's early development before withdrawing from public involvement in 2010.

equipment.title: The Underlying Technical Standards
equipment.paragraph: Bitcoin's Proof of Work relies on the SHA-256 cryptographic hash function, originally designed by the US National Security Agency and published as a federal standard; solving it at scale today is typically done with purpose-built hardware called ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits) rather than general-purpose computers. Ethereum and other Proof-of-Stake networks replace that hardware race with validator software run on ordinary servers, backed financially by staked coins instead of computational work.

modernDevelopments.title: Where the Technology Stands Today
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Ethereum's move from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake in September 2022, an upgrade known as "the Merge," cut the network's energy consumption by more than 99% according to the Ethereum Foundation's own published estimates. Layer-2 networks that process transactions off the main blockchain and settle the results back onto it have become a major focus for improving transaction speed and cost. Meanwhile, a growing number of central banks are researching or piloting central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) — a related but structurally different concept, since a CBDC is issued and controlled by a central monetary authority rather than a decentralized network.

intro.title: What Is the Foreign Exchange Market?
intro.paragraph1: The foreign exchange market — commonly called forex or FX — is the global, decentralized marketplace where one currency is exchanged for another. It has no single physical location or central exchange; instead, it operates as a network of banks, central banks, brokers, and financial institutions trading directly with one another around the clock on business days, from Sydney and Tokyo through London to New York.
intro.paragraph2: According to the Bank for International Settlements' 2025 Triennial Central Bank Survey, average daily turnover in the global FX market reached approximately $9.5 trillion in April 2025, making it by a wide margin the largest and most liquid financial market in the world.
intro.disclaimer: The figures and explanations on this page are educational only and do not constitute investment advice or a recommendation to trade any currency.

history.title: A Brief History of the Global Exchange Rate System
history.paragraph1: For most of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, major currencies were pegged to a fixed weight of gold under the classical gold standard, which gave exchange rates long stretches of stability at the cost of tying domestic monetary policy to gold flows. That system broke down during the Great Depression and the Second World War.
history.paragraph2: In July 1944, representatives of 44 Allied nations meeting at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, agreed on a new system: the US dollar was pegged to gold at $35 per ounce, and every other member currency was pegged to the dollar within a narrow band, with the newly created International Monetary Fund overseeing adjustments. The system held through the 1950s and 1960s, but persistent US balance-of-payments deficits eventually made the gold peg unsustainable. On August 15, 1971, President Richard Nixon suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, an event now known as the 'Nixon Shock.' By March 1973, the major economies had abandoned fixed rates altogether in favor of the floating exchange rate system still in place today, in which most currency values are set by market supply and demand rather than a government-fixed peg.

diagram.caption: A simplified timeline of the modern international exchange rate system, from the Bretton Woods peg to today's mostly floating regime.

regimes.title: Exchange Rate Regimes Today
regimes.intro: Not every currency is priced by the market in the same way. Governments and central banks choose from several regimes, each with different trade-offs between stability and monetary independence.

The exchange rate moves within a range influenced by market forces, but the central bank actively intervenes to guide it toward a target.

risks.title: Understanding Currency Risk
risks.paragraph1: Exchange rates move continuously in response to interest rate decisions, inflation data, trade balances, political events, and shifts in market sentiment, which is why the same amount of money can buy a different quantity of foreign currency from one day to the next.
risks.paragraph2: Retail currency trading typically involves leverage, which magnifies both potential gains and potential losses relative to the amount actually deposited, and most retail traders who use leveraged forex products lose money over time according to disclosures published by regulated brokers themselves.
risks.paragraph3: Anyone converting or holding foreign currency should also be aware of counterparty risk (the reliability of the bank or broker involved), settlement risk, and the spread between buy and sell prices, which is where most currency-exchange providers make their revenue.

items.question: Why is the Saudi riyal's rate against the dollar always the same number?
items.answer: The Saudi riyal has been formally pegged to the US dollar at 3.75 riyals per dollar since 1986, and the Saudi Central Bank maintains that peg by buying and selling dollars as needed — so unlike a freely floating currency, its rate against the dollar does not fluctuate day to day.

items.question: What's the difference between the mid-market rate shown here and the rate a bank or exchange office offers?
items.answer: The rate on this page is the mid-market rate — the midpoint between global buy and sell prices, with no markup. Banks, exchange offices, and payment apps typically add a spread or fee on top of this rate, so the amount actually received when exchanging money in person or online is usually somewhat less favorable.

history.title: History and Origins
history.paragraph: Organized currency trading is far older than modern electronic markets: merchant banking houses exchanged bills of currency across European trade fairs as early as the Middle Ages, and by the 19th century, London had become the world's dominant foreign exchange center, underpinned by the gold standard and the Bank of England. Electronic trading transformed the market from the 1970s onward, following the shift to floating exchange rates, and today the vast majority of global FX turnover is executed electronically between banks, funds, and increasingly automated trading systems.

equipment.title: Standards and Infrastructure
equipment.paragraph: Every currency traded worldwide is identified by a standardized three-letter code defined in ISO 4217, the international standard maintained since 1978 to remove ambiguity between currencies that share a symbol, such as the dollar sign used by more than 20 different currencies. Cross-border payment messages between banks are typically routed over the SWIFT network, while settlement of the trades themselves is increasingly handled through CLS (Continuous Linked Settlement), a specialized settlement system founded in 2002 to eliminate the risk that one side of a currency trade pays out while the other side fails to deliver.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Today's forex market is dominated by electronic communication networks and algorithmic trading, with a large and growing share of spot trading executed by automated systems rather than human dealers. Central banks are separately exploring central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), which could eventually change how cross-border settlement itself works, while instant-payment initiatives are pushing to shorten the multi-day settlement times that still apply to many traditional currency transfers.

intro.title: What Are Commodity Markets?
intro.paragraph1: A commodity is a raw material or primary good — a precious metal, an energy source, or an agricultural product — that is largely interchangeable regardless of who produced it: a barrel of WTI crude or a troy ounce of LBMA-standard gold is priced the same worldwide, unlike a differentiated product such as a car or a smartphone. Commodities trade on organized exchanges and over-the-counter markets, with prices set by the same forces as any other market: supply, demand, and how participants expect both to change.
intro.paragraph2: Gold and silver prices have been on a sustained climb through 2026, with gold trading near record highs and up more than 25% since early 2025 amid interest-rate expectations and safe-haven demand, according to market reporting — a reminder that, like any traded asset, commodity prices move continuously rather than holding a single fixed value.
intro.disclaimer: The figures and explanations on this page are educational only and do not constitute investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any commodity.

pricing.title: How Commodity Prices Are Determined
pricing.paragraph1: Gold and silver's global reference prices are set through the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) Gold and Silver Price auctions — electronic, twice-daily (gold) and once-daily (silver) auctions where dealers submit buy and sell orders until the price that clears the market is found. Oil has no single global auction; instead, futures contracts for WTI (traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange) and Brent (traded on the Intercontinental Exchange) serve as the reference benchmarks most other crude oil is priced against.
pricing.paragraph2: In every case, the underlying logic is the same supply-and-demand relationship taught in introductory economics: at any given moment, there is a quantity producers are willing to supply at each price and a quantity buyers are willing to demand at each price, and the market price settles at the point where those two quantities are equal — the equilibrium.

risks.title: Understanding Commodity Risk
risks.paragraph1: Commodity prices are historically more volatile than many other asset classes, moving sharply on production disruptions, shifts in industrial demand, currency movements, and geopolitical events — the same amount of gold, silver, or oil can be worth a meaningfully different amount from one week to the next.
risks.paragraph2: Holding a physical commodity carries costs the spot price itself doesn't show: storage, insurance, and — for gold and silver bought as jewelry or coins — a retail markup over the spot price that can be substantial and varies by purity, craftsmanship, and dealer.
risks.paragraph3: Trading commodities through futures or leveraged products magnifies both potential gains and potential losses relative to the amount actually deposited, and most retail traders who use leveraged products lose money over time according to disclosures published by regulated brokers themselves.

items.question: Why does the gold price shown here differ from the price at my local jewelry shop?
items.answer: This page shows the spot price of pure (24-karat / 999.9 fine) gold. Jewelry is typically a lower purity (like 21-karat or 18-karat, which contain less actual gold per gram) and includes the maker's craftsmanship and the shop's retail markup on top of the spot price — so the two numbers are expected to differ.

items.question: What's the difference between a troy ounce and a regular ounce?
items.answer: Precious metals are priced in troy ounces, an older unit still used specifically for gold and silver, equal to about 31.1 grams. A regular (avoirdupois) ounce, the one used for everyday weight, is smaller — about 28.35 grams — so converting between the two matters if you're comparing a metal price to a weight given in ordinary ounces.

A fixed 7-day gold trend was the honest choice that fits within that limit — see the project's public roadmap for the plan to revisit this after launch.

items.question: Is WTI or Brent the "correct" oil price?
items.answer: Neither — they're both legitimate benchmarks for different crude oil grades and regions. WTI reflects US domestic crude, while Brent reflects crude produced in the North Sea and is the more widely referenced benchmark for crude priced outside the Americas. This page shows WTI for the converter and quick figures.

history.title: History and Origins
history.paragraph: Gold has functioned as a store of value across civilizations for millennia, from ancient Egyptian gold artifacts to the first standardized gold coins minted in the kingdom of Lydia around the 6th century BCE — and it later anchored the classical gold standard and the Bretton Woods system before the world moved to floating exchange rates in the 1970s. Silver shared a similar monetary role for much of history, often circulating alongside gold as coinage, before industrial demand became its dominant use in the modern era. The modern oil industry is conventionally dated to 1859, when Edwin Drake drilled the first commercially successful oil well in Titusville, Pennsylvania, launching an industry that would go on to reshape the 20th century global economy.

equipment.title: Standards and Measurement
equipment.paragraph: Gold and silver purity is expressed either in karats (24-karat is pure gold; 21-karat, common in Gulf jewelry markets, is 21 parts gold to 3 parts other metals) or in fineness — parts per thousand, where 999.9 fine means 99.99% pure. Bars traded on the LBMA market must meet its 'Good Delivery' standard: approximately 400-troy-ounce bars of at least 995 fineness, produced by an LBMA-accredited refiner. Crude oil, meanwhile, is classified partly by API gravity (a measure of density — 'light' crude like WTI is less dense and generally easier to refine than 'heavy' crude) and by sulfur content ('sweet' crude has less sulfur than 'sour' crude).

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Gold-backed exchange-traded funds, first launched in the early 2000s, let investors gain price exposure to gold without arranging physical storage, and have since become one of the largest sources of investment demand for the metal. In oil markets, the growth of US shale production over the past two decades reshaped global supply dynamics, while OPEC+ — the expanded alliance of OPEC members and other major producers including Russia — has taken on a larger coordinating role in managing global supply since 2016.

intro.title: How Weather Forecasting Works
intro.paragraph1: A weather forecast is a scientific estimate of future atmospheric conditions, built by feeding millions of real-time observations — from weather stations, balloons, satellites, ships, and aircraft — into physics-based computer models that simulate how the atmosphere will evolve over the coming hours and days. These are called numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, and they solve the same fundamental equations of fluid motion and thermodynamics that govern how air, moisture, and heat move around the planet.
intro.paragraph2: Forecast accuracy naturally decreases the further out it looks: short-range forecasts (today, tomorrow) are usually quite reliable, while forecasts a week or more out capture general trends rather than precise details, because tiny uncertainties in today's starting conditions grow over time — a phenomenon formally described by chaos theory.

diagram.caption: The water cycle: the continuous movement of water between the surface and the atmosphere that drives clouds and precipitation.

models.title: Weather Models and Data Sources
models.paragraph1: This tool's forecasts are sourced from Open-Meteo, which blends output from several national weather agencies' numerical models — including the US National Weather Service's GFS, the German Weather Service's ICON, and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' IFS — selecting the best available model for each location and refreshing as new model runs complete.
models.paragraph2: Each model divides the atmosphere into a three-dimensional grid and calculates how temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind will change at every grid point over time; a model's resolution (the distance between grid points) directly affects how much local detail — like an individual mountain valley or coastline — it can represent.
models.paragraph3: Because these models depend on real-time observational data, forecast quality tends to be best in regions with dense weather station and satellite coverage, and can be somewhat less precise in remote areas with sparser observations.

items.question: How accurate are these forecasts?
items.answer: Forecasts for today and tomorrow are generally quite reliable, typically accurate to within a degree or two of temperature. Accuracy drops the further out a forecast looks — a 7-day forecast should be read as a general trend rather than a precise prediction for that specific day.

items.question: How often is the data updated?
items.answer: The underlying weather models this tool draws on are refreshed hourly to every few hours depending on the model, and this page refreshes its own cached data roughly once an hour.

items.question: Why does the forecast for my city sometimes change from one visit to the next?
items.answer: Forecasts are recalculated every time new observational data comes in, so a forecast for the same future date can shift somewhat as the model incorporates newer information — this is completely normal, and forecasts generally become more precise the closer they get to the date in question.

items.question: What does "feels like" temperature mean?
items.answer: The "feels like" (apparent) temperature accounts for factors beyond the raw air temperature — mainly wind and humidity — that affect how warm or cold a human body actually perceives the air to be.

items.question: Does this tool provide severe weather warnings?
items.answer: No. This tool intentionally does not include live severe-weather alerts or disaster warnings (hurricanes, wildfires, and similar). For official warnings, always consult your local national meteorological agency or emergency services.

history.title: History and Origins
history.paragraph: Modern meteorology traces back to Robert FitzRoy, the British naval officer and scientist who established the UK's Meteorological Office in 1854 and is generally credited with coining the term "weather forecast," publishing the first daily forecasts in The Times in 1861 based on telegraph reports from coastal observation stations. The scientific foundation for today's computer-based forecasting came from Lewis Fry Richardson, who in 1922 proposed calculating future weather by numerically solving the physical equations governing the atmosphere — a method too slow to do by hand, but validated in 1950 when a team including Jule Charney and John von Neumann ran the first successful computer-based forecast on the ENIAC computer, launching the field of numerical weather prediction that all modern forecasts still build on.

intro.title: Understanding BMR and TDEE
intro.paragraph1: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the number of calories your body burns at complete rest just to keep its basic functions running — breathing, circulation, cell repair, and maintaining body temperature. Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE) builds on that by adding the calories burned through daily movement and exercise, giving a fuller picture of how many calories your body actually uses in a typical day.
intro.paragraph2: Body weight changes according to a simple energy-balance principle: consuming more calories than TDEE over time leads to weight gain, consuming fewer leads to weight loss, and matching TDEE roughly maintains weight. This tool uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation by default — the equation most commonly recommended in clinical practice — with an option to switch to the Katch-McArdle equation if you know your body fat percentage, which tends to be more accurate for people with an above-average muscle mass.

diagram.caption: When calories in and calories out are balanced, body weight tends to stay roughly stable; tipping either side shifts it up or down over time.

items.question: Why does my BMR differ between the Mifflin-St Jeor and Katch-McArdle results?
items.answer: Mifflin-St Jeor estimates BMR from your total weight, height, age, and sex. Katch-McArdle instead uses your lean body mass directly, so it tends to give a higher, more accurate result for people who are visibly more muscular than average, and a lower one for people with a higher body fat percentage than average — since muscle burns more calories at rest than fat tissue does.

items.question: How accurate are these calorie estimates?
items.answer: Predictive equations like Mifflin-St Jeor are estimates validated against population averages, typically accurate to within about 10% for most people — not an exact measurement of your individual metabolism, which can only be measured directly through indirect calorimetry.

items.question: Why does the tool warn me about an "aggressive" deficit or surplus?
items.answer: A very large calorie deficit increases the risk of losing muscle mass along with fat and can be hard to sustain, while a very large surplus typically leads to a higher proportion of fat gain relative to muscle. Keeping the daily adjustment within a moderate range relative to your TDEE is a widely recommended approach for a more sustainable pace of change.

items.question: Should I recalculate my TDEE as my weight changes?
items.answer: Yes — BMR and TDEE both scale with body weight, so it's reasonable to recalculate every several weeks or after a meaningful weight change, rather than relying on a single calculation indefinitely.

items.question: Does this account for factors like medical conditions or medications?
items.answer: No. This tool applies general population-based equations and does not account for medical conditions, certain medications, or other individual factors that can meaningfully affect metabolism — a healthcare professional can account for those.

history.title: History and Origins
history.paragraph: The scientific effort to estimate resting energy expenditure from body measurements dates back to the Harris-Benedict equation, published in 1918-1919 from data on around 250 subjects — for decades the standard formula used in clinical and research settings. In 1990, a team led by Mark Mifflin and Sachiko St Jeor re-derived the equation from a larger, more contemporary sample of 498 subjects measured by indirect calorimetry, finding it predicted resting energy expenditure more accurately than the original Harris-Benedict formula for the modern population — it has since become the equation most commonly recommended by dietetic professional bodies.

modernDevelopments.title: Modern Developments
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Indirect calorimetry — measuring the oxygen a person consumes and the carbon dioxide they produce to directly calculate energy expenditure — remains the clinical gold standard where a predictive equation isn't precise enough, such as in hospital nutrition support. Outside clinical settings, consumer wearable devices now estimate daily energy expenditure continuously using heart rate and movement data, though their accuracy varies significantly by device and activity type compared to laboratory measurement.

intro.title: Understanding Compound Interest
intro.paragraph1: Compound interest is interest calculated not only on the original amount deposited or invested — the principal — but also on the interest that has already accumulated in previous periods. Once interest is added to a balance, the next period's interest is calculated on that larger amount, so the balance grows faster and faster over time rather than by a fixed amount each period, which is how simple interest works instead.
intro.paragraph2: Three factors accelerate this growth beyond the interest rate itself: the compounding frequency (how often interest is added to the balance — daily compounding grows a balance slightly faster than annual compounding at the same stated rate, since interest starts earning its own interest sooner), the length of time the money is left to grow (the effect compounds most visibly in later years, not early ones), and regular contributions added along the way, each of which then earns its own compounding return for however long it remains invested. This tool models all three by simulating the balance month by month, applying the chosen compounding frequency's monthly-equivalent rate and adding any monthly contribution before moving to the next month.

items.question: What's the difference between compound interest and simple interest?
items.answer: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal every period, so it adds the same fixed amount each time. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus all previously earned interest, so the amount it adds grows larger each period — a difference that becomes dramatic over long time horizons even at the same stated rate.

items.question: How much does compounding frequency actually matter?
items.answer: Less than most people expect at typical rates. Switching from annual to daily compounding on the same stated annual rate increases the effective growth by only a small fraction of a percentage point per year — meaningful over decades, but far smaller in effect than raising the interest rate, extending the time horizon, or increasing contributions.

items.question: Why does the order interest and contributions are applied matter?
items.answer: This calculator applies each month's interest to the existing balance first, then adds that month's contribution — a common convention that matches how many savings and brokerage accounts credit interest relative to when a periodic deposit posts. A contribution made at the very start of a month instead of the end would compound for one additional month and produce a very slightly higher result.

items.question: Is it realistic to assume a fixed annual rate every year?
items.answer: No — this is the tool's most important simplification. Savings accounts and CDs often do pay a fairly stable rate, but investments like stocks and mutual funds have returns that vary significantly year to year; a fixed "average" rate here is a simplified projection, not a guarantee, and real returns will follow a bumpier path even when the long-run average matches the rate entered.

items.question: Why does starting earlier matter so much, even with smaller contributions?
items.answer: Because each dollar invested earns compounding returns for a longer stretch of time, and that stretch of time compounds multiplicatively rather than just adding up — money invested a decade earlier can end up worth substantially more than a much larger sum invested a decade later, purely because it had more compounding periods to grow through.

history.title: The First Book Devoted Entirely to Compound Interest
history.paragraph: Compound interest itself long predates any book about it — Babylonian clay tablets already record interest-bearing loans, and many ancient legal codes limited or banned it outright as usury. What changed in the early modern period was the emergence of dedicated mathematical tools for calculating it. Italian mathematician Luca Pacioli's 1494 Summa de Arithmetica included one of the earliest known references to the "Rule of 72" — a mental-math shortcut for estimating how many years it takes an investment to double at a given compound rate. The subject then got its own dedicated textbook in 1613, when London mathematics practitioner Richard Witt published Arithmeticall Questions — widely regarded as the first English-language book devoted entirely to compound interest, containing 124 worked examples and printed tables for valuing annuities, leases, and property purchases at various rates.

modernDevelopments.title: From Printed Tables to Automated Investing
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For centuries after Witt, anyone who needed a compound-interest calculation by hand relied on printed reference tables — bulky books listing the growth factor for common combinations of rate and term. Financial calculators and then spreadsheets replaced those tables in the 20th century, and today robo-advisors and micro-investing apps go a step further, automatically depositing a fixed contribution on a schedule — a strategy often called dollar-cost averaging — and reinvesting the returns without any manual calculation at all, the same monthly-contribution-plus-compounding structure this calculator models.

intro.title: Understanding Loan Amortization
intro.paragraph1: A personal or auto loan is typically repaid through fixed, equal monthly payments over a set term — a structure called an amortizing loan. Even though every payment is the same size, the mix inside it changes constantly: early payments are weighted heavily toward interest, since interest is charged on the full outstanding balance, while later payments are weighted toward principal, since the balance — and the interest charged on it — has shrunk.
intro.paragraph2: The monthly payment itself is calculated so that the loan reaches a zero balance exactly at the end of the term, given the loan amount and interest rate. Unlike a mortgage, a personal or auto loan calculated here has no mortgage insurance, property tax, or homeowners association fee built in — its cost is just the interest charged on the declining balance over the term you choose.

items.question: Why does more of my payment go toward interest at the beginning of the loan?
items.answer: Interest is calculated each month on whatever balance remains, and early on that balance is at its highest — so the interest portion of a fixed payment starts large and shrinks every month as the balance falls, while the principal portion does the opposite.

items.question: What's the difference between a personal loan and an auto loan calculation-wise?
items.answer: Mathematically nothing — both are standard fixed-rate installment loans amortized the same way this calculator models. The practical differences are that an auto loan is secured by the vehicle (usually giving it a lower rate) while an unsecured personal loan typically carries a higher rate to compensate the lender for the added risk.

items.question: Does this calculator include fees like an origination fee or dealer add-ons?
items.answer: No — it calculates payments from the loan amount, rate, and term alone. Real loans often carry additional costs (an origination fee on many personal loans, or dealer-added products on an auto loan) that increase what you actually pay beyond this estimate; ask a lender for the loan's full APR, which is required by law to include most such fees.

items.question: Why does paying off a loan early save interest?
items.answer: Because interest accrues only on the outstanding balance for as long as it's outstanding — an extra payment applied directly to principal shrinks that balance immediately, so every future month accrues interest on a smaller amount, cutting the total interest paid over the life of the loan.

items.question: How does the loan term affect my total cost?
items.answer: A longer term lowers the monthly payment by spreading the same principal over more payments, but it also means the balance stays higher for longer and accrues interest for more months — so a longer term usually means a lower payment but a higher total amount paid over the life of the loan.

history.title: How Installment Credit Put Cars — and Everything Else — Within Reach
history.paragraph: Before the 20th century, borrowing to buy an everyday consumer good was rare and often frowned upon; big purchases were typically saved for and paid in cash. That changed with the automobile. In 1919, General Motors founded the General Motors Acceptance Corporation (GMAC) specifically to let dealers finance their inventory and let customers buy a car on an installment plan rather than paying the full price upfront. The approach caught on fast: by 1930, most durable goods in the United States — including more than two-thirds of all automobiles sold — were bought on some form of installment credit, and GMAC's model became the template for the captive auto-finance companies still owned by automakers today.

modernDevelopments.title: From the Dealership Finance Office to Instant Online Approval
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For most of the 20th century, arranging a personal or auto loan meant a trip to a bank, credit union, or dealership finance office and a paper application. Online peer-to-peer and marketplace lenders that emerged in the mid-2000s were among the first to let a borrower apply for and receive a personal-loan decision entirely online, and that model has since become mainstream: many banks, credit unions, and auto dealers now offer instant or same-day automated approval by pulling a credit report and running the underwriting decision the moment an application is submitted, compressing a process that once took days into a matter of minutes.

intro.title: How Time Zones Work
intro.paragraph1: The Earth rotates once every 24 hours, so different longitudes face the sun at different moments — noon in one place is midnight on the opposite side of the planet. Rather than every location keeping its own precise solar time, the world is divided into time zones: bands that share a single, standardized offset from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the modern reference successor to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).
intro.paragraph2: This tool computes every conversion locally, using the Intl.DateTimeFormat API built into every modern browser — the same IANA time zone database that powers phones, servers, and operating systems worldwide, with no external service, no network request, and no usage limit.

dst.title: Daylight Saving Time: Why Clocks Change
dst.paragraph1: Daylight saving time (DST) shifts clocks forward by one hour in spring and back in autumn, aligning waking hours more closely with daylight during the months when days are longer. It was first proposed seriously by New Zealand entomologist George Vernon Hudson in 1895 and by British builder William Willett in 1907, and was first adopted at a national scale by Germany and Austria-Hungary in 1916, during World War I, as a fuel-saving measure.
dst.paragraph2: Its use today is far from universal: most of Asia, Africa, and an increasing number of countries no longer observe it, while the European Union and several US states have active proposals to abolish the twice-yearly clock change and adopt a single, permanent offset instead. Because it's a political decision, not an astronomical one, this tool always reflects whatever rule is currently in effect for a given zone via the browser's own, regularly updated time zone data — never a hardcoded assumption.

items.question: Is a time zone the same as a UTC offset?
items.answer: Not exactly. A UTC offset is just a number (e.g., +03:00); a time zone is a named region (e.g., Asia/Riyadh) that maps to a specific offset, or a sequence of offsets over the year if it observes daylight saving time. Two time zones can share the same offset today and diverge on a DST transition date.

items.question: Why do some time zones use a 30- or 45-minute offset?
items.answer: A handful of countries chose an offset that isn't a whole hour from UTC when they set their standard time — India (UTC+5:30) and Nepal (UTC+5:45) are the best-known examples — usually to better match the country's actual longitude or to align with a historical local mean time.

items.question: What is UTC, and how is it different from GMT?
items.answer: UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) is the modern time standard, kept by atomic clocks and coordinated internationally. GMT (Greenwich Mean Time) is the older, astronomically defined standard it replaced. In practice, the two are within a fraction of a second of each other and are used interchangeably for most everyday purposes, including this tool.

items.question: Why does this tool only let me search from a fixed list of cities?
items.answer: Every listed city maps to a specific IANA time zone identifier — the actual unit your browser understands. Many cities within the same country share one zone (all of mainland China, for example, uses a single Beijing-based zone), so the list represents zones through their most recognizable city rather than listing every city individually.

items.question: Can the time difference between two cities change during the year?
items.answer: Yes, whenever the two cities don't observe daylight saving time on the same schedule — or one observes it and the other doesn't. The gap between London and New York, for instance, is 5 hours most of the year, but briefly narrows to 4 hours for a few weeks each spring and autumn while only one of them has shifted its clocks.

history.title: The Origin of Standardized Time Zones
history.paragraph: Before railways, every town kept its own local solar time, which was harmless when travel was slow but caused real scheduling chaos once trains could cross multiple time meridians in a single day. Scottish-Canadian engineer Sandford Fleming proposed a worldwide system of standard time zones in 1878-79, built around a single global reference meridian. That proposal was formalized at the International Meridian Conference held in Washington, D.C. in October 1884, which selected the Greenwich meridian in London as the universal reference point (0°) from which all other zones would be measured.

equipment.title: The Technical Standards Behind It
equipment.paragraph: Modern civil time is kept in practice by atomic clocks, which measure time via the extremely stable vibration frequency of cesium atoms, accurate to within about one second every 100 million years. The globally coordinated result, UTC, is maintained by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in Paris. Software applies UTC to a specific location using the IANA Time Zone Database (tz database) — the record of every zone's historical and current offset and DST rules that browsers, operating systems, and servers download and use, and which this tool reads directly through Intl.DateTimeFormat.

modernDevelopments.title: Where Things Stand Today
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Political debate over daylight saving time has intensified in recent years: the European Parliament voted in 2019 to end the mandatory clock change across EU member states, though implementation has repeatedly stalled over disagreement on which permanent offset each country should keep; several individual US states have passed conditional legislation to adopt permanent daylight time pending federal approval. Meanwhile, the IANA tz database itself is updated several times a year as governments change zone boundaries or DST rules — exactly why software that reads it live, rather than relying on a fixed table, stays accurate without needing an update of its own.

intro.title: Understanding Percentages
intro.paragraph1: A percentage expresses a number as a fraction of 100 — the word itself comes from the Latin per centum, "by the hundred." Writing a value as a percentage makes it easy to compare quantities of very different sizes on the same scale: whether a class has 20 or 200 students, saying 15% failed a test conveys the same relative information either way.
intro.paragraph2: This tool covers five distinct percentage calculations that are frequently confused with one another: finding a percentage of a number, finding what percentage one number is of another, percentage change (a directional comparison that uses the original value as its base), reverse percentage (working backward from a known result to the original number), and percentage difference (a symmetric comparison that does not treat either value as the "original").

diagram.caption: 27 of these 100 squares are shaded — this is literally what "27%" means: 27 parts for every 100.

intro.paragraph3: The distinction between percentage change and percentage difference trips up even experienced analysts. Going from 80 to 100 is a percentage change of +25%, using 80 (the original value) as the base. But the percentage difference between the same two numbers, which uses their average of 90 as the base instead, is about 22.2% — the same two numbers, two different questions, two different valid answers.
